Statuspage.io Pricing: Hidden Costs & Caveats Explained

# Statuspage.io Pricing: Hidden Costs & Caveats Explained

Leo Baecker / July 23, 2026 / Comparisons

Status pages backed by real monitoring.

Detect, communicate and resolve incidents from the same workspace.

Statuspage pricing starts at $29 per month for the Hobby plan, but that number covers a single public page with email-only notifications and no monitoring behind it. Statuspage (the Atlassian product, formerly statuspage.io) actually maintains three separate price lists: public pages from $29 to $1,499+/mo, private pages from $79 to $1,499+/mo, and audience-specific pages from $300/mo. Each page type is billed on its own, and none of them detect outages, so a monitoring tool is a separate line on your budget.

This guide breaks down every Statuspage plan with current numbers, explains what drives the bill up (subscriber counts, feature gates, and the multi-page-type model), shares what reviewers say about the cost, and covers where Hyperping fits as a flat-rate option that bundles the monitoring Statuspage leaves out.

In this guide:

- What every Statuspage plan costs, across public, private, and audience-specific pages
- The feature gates that push teams up tiers (SMS at $99, full customization at $399)
- What a realistic "Statuspage plus monitoring plus on-call" stack costs
- What G2 reviewers say about the pricing, in their own words
- How to keep a Statuspage bill down, and when to switch instead

## Quick summary

- Public pages run $29 (Hobby) to $399 (Business) to $1,499+ (Enterprise) per month, with a free plan limited to 100 subscribers and 2 team members. Tiers are driven by subscribers, team members, and metrics, not by how much product you use.
- Private pages are a separate subscription, from $79 (Starter) to $599 (Corporate) and beyond. A company with one customer-facing page and one internal page pays two bills.
- Key features sit behind tier gates. SMS and webhook notifications require the $99/mo Startup plan. Full CSS/HTML/JS customization and component subscriptions require the $399/mo Business plan.
- There is no monitoring. Statuspage cannot tell whether your API is up. Teams pair it with Pingdom or similar, plus an on-call tool, which pushes a realistic stack past $600/mo.
- Reviewers like the product and flag the price. The most consistent complaints on G2 are subscriber-based cost scaling, the mandatory Atlassian account system, and paying premium prices for a communication-only tool.
- Hyperping covers status pages, monitoring, and on-call from $29/mo flat, with private pages at $89/mo, as one subscription instead of three tools.

Pricing figures are based on Atlassian's published rates as of July 2026 and may change. Check the official Statuspage pricing page for current numbers.

## Is Statuspage pricing actually worth it?

Statuspage was the pioneer of the status page category, and it still carries the trust that comes with that. Reviewers consistently describe it as reliable and simple to operate during an incident, which is exactly when you need those qualities. For enterprises already paying for Jira Service Management and the rest of the Atlassian stack, the integration story can justify the price.

The value question gets harder for everyone else. You are paying $29 to $399 a month for a communication layer only: no uptime checks, no on-call, no alerting when something breaks. The tiers scale on subscriber and team member counts, so the bill grows as your customer base grows even though the product does not change. And the moment you want an internal page next to your public one, you start a second subscription on a second price list.

That mismatch, premium pricing for a narrow job, is the main reason teams go looking for Statuspage alternatives. The rest of this guide puts numbers on it.

## Why listen to us?

I am Léo, founder of Hyperping. The disclosure up front: Hyperping competes directly with Statuspage, so I have a stake in this comparison. I will be straight about where Statuspage is the better fit, because there are real cases where it is.

For this guide I went through Atlassian's published pricing for all three page types, read through Statuspage's G2 reviews (the pricing complaints repeat with unusual consistency), and priced out the full stack teams actually run around it. Where the numbers could change, I have dated them.

## What is Statuspage?

Statuspage is a hosted status page product from Atlassian. It gives you a public or private page where you post incidents, scheduled maintenance, and component health, and it notifies subscribers by email, SMS, or webhook when something changes. It integrates with the Atlassian ecosystem, most usefully Jira Service Management, and offers a REST API, incident templates, and third-party component embedding.

What it does not do is monitoring. Statuspage has no way to check whether a service responds. Every status shown on the page comes from a human, an API call, or an integration with a separate monitoring tool. One 5-star G2 reviewer, otherwise a fan, named this as their only complaint: "It doesn't have an automated system to check if a service is accessible or it responds with a 200 OK status code."

## Statuspage pricing breakdown

Statuspage prices by page type. Public, private, and audience-specific pages each have their own plan ladder, and each page you run is its own subscription. Billing is monthly by default; yearly billing exists but requires going through Atlassian support to set up.

### Public pages: $0 to $1,499+/mo

Public pages are what most people mean by "a status page." Tiers scale on subscribers, team members, and metrics.

| Plan | Monthly | Subscribers | Team members | Metrics | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Free | $0 | 100 | 2 | 2 | 25 components, email notifications, rate-limited API |
| Hobby | $29 | 250 | 5 | 5 | Custom domain, basic customization, email only |
| Startup | $99 | 1,000 | 10 | 10 | Adds SMS + webhook notifications, custom CSS, team SSO |
| Business | $399 | 5,000 | 25 | 25 | Full CSS/HTML/JS, component subscriptions |
| Enterprise | $1,499+ | 25,000 | 50 | 50 | Higher limits, enhanced support, PO/invoicing |

Two gates in this table drive most upgrades. If you want subscribers notified by SMS or webhook instead of email only, the floor is Startup at $99. If you want full control over how the page looks (CSS, HTML, JS) or per-component subscriptions, the floor is Business at $399.

### Private pages: $79 to $1,499+/mo

Private pages sit behind authentication (SAML 2.0 with Okta and similar IdPs) and are aimed at internal audiences. They are priced separately from public pages, on their own ladder.

| Plan | Monthly | Authenticated users | Team members | Metrics |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Starter | $79 | 50 | 5 | 5 |
| Growth | $249 | 300 | 15 | 15 |
| Corporate | $599 | 1,000 | 35 | 35 |
| Enterprise | $1,499+ | 5,000+ | 50 | Higher |

The practical consequence: a team that wants a customer-facing page and an internal page for employees pays for both. A common mid-market pairing, Startup public plus Growth private, is $348/mo before any monitoring or alerting tool enters the picture.

### Audience-specific pages: from $300/mo

Audience-specific pages show different components and statuses to different user groups from one page, instead of forcing you to run several separate pages. Pricing is volume-tiered:

- Base tier: $300/mo for 500 users, 10 groups, 25 team members, and 30 metrics
- Tiers 2 to 10 add $200 each, tiers 11 to 30 add $100 each, tiers 31+ add $50 each

Allocations are fixed per tier with no flexibility inside a tier, so a small overage in users can mean a full tier step up.
